title: GE90 T25 sensor housing: the first certified printed engine part
facts: Housing for the compressor-inlet temperature and pressure sensor of the GE90-94B (Boeing 777) | Protects the sensor electronics from icing and punishing airflow | Retrofit approved by the FAA in 2015; opened the way for the LEAP nozzle
gains: Fast prototype-to-production; first certified printed engine part
challenges: First of its kind: new process specification and FAA acceptance
picture_source: ge.com › news › “The FAA cleared the first 3D printed part to fly”

title: GE9X: printed TiAl low-pressure turbine blades
facts: Low-pressure turbine blades printed at Avio Aero, Cameri (Italy) | 304 parts in 7 printed components on each GE9X | Engine FAA-certified September 2020 (Boeing 777X)
printer: Arcam, now Colibrium: A2X (6 blades/batch), Spectra H (10)
gains: Blades about half the weight of nickel; key to −10% fuel vs GE90
challenges: TiAl is brittle and fussy, EBM is demanding; 62 machines for rate
sources: GE Additive / Metal AM, June 2019; CompositesWorld; GE Aerospace, Sept 2020
picture: GE9X TiAl LPT blade / Arcam machines at Cameri

title: UEC VK-1600V: up to 70% of castings replaced by printed parts
facts: Helicopter engine for the Ka-62, designed entirely in 3D (no paper drawings) at UEC-Klimov | Up to 70% of castings printed, incl. hot-section parts and the first-support housing (made with UEC’s Chernyshev plant, Moscow) | 1,400 hp take-off, 210 kg dry weight; demonstrator 2021
printer: Rostec Additive Technologies Center: Russia’s largest laser machine, Russian materials
gains: Lead time from 6 months to 3 weeks; lighter parts
challenges: Type certificate planned for 2023 and series for 2024: current status unclear
sources: Rostec/UEC, May 2021; Airframer; Rostec ATC, May 2021; www1.ru, Nov 2024

title: Liebherr-Aerospace: printed spoiler-actuator valve block
facts: First printed primary-flight-control hydraulic part flown on an Airbus (A380 test flight, 30 March 2017) | Same performance as the forged titanium valve block | Then serial A350 parts: nose-gear bracket (2019), cargo-door actuator and valve (2022), flex shaft
company: Liebherr-Aerospace (Lindenberg, DE; HQ Toulouse) with TU Chemnitz
gains: 35% lighter, fewer parts, minimal titanium waste
challenges: Whole chain still to optimise: powder, laser parameters, post-processing

technology: Laser powder bed and wire DED · titanium
title: Airbus A350: from printed brackets to 7-metre titanium parts
facts: 2017: first printed titanium bracket on a series Airbus (Arconic, Austin) | 2026: plasma wire-DED titanium parts in the A350 cargo-door surround | Near-net-shape parts up to 7 m long, then machined
company: Airbus with Arconic (now Howmet) and Norsk Titanium
printer: Laser powder bed and e-beam (Arconic); plasma wire DED
gains: Avoids recycling 80–95% of bought titanium; weeks instead of months
challenges: Ultrasonic inspection and machining still needed; energy sources still evaluated
sources: Howmet/Arconic, Sept 2017; Airbus newsroom and Metal AM, Jan 2026

title: Boeing 787: Norsk Titanium structural parts
facts: Rapid Plasma Deposition: titanium wire melted by plasma torches | First FAA-approved printed structural titanium parts (Feb 2017) | Initial family of four parts near the rear of the cabin
company: Norsk Titanium (Norway; Plattsburgh, NY) for Boeing
challenges: Preforms must be machined; parts approved one by one until the process is approved
sources: Norsk Titanium / Business Wire, Apr 2017; Engadget; Aero-Mag
picture: Norsk Titanium RPD part, as-deposited vs machined

title: COMAC C919: printed titanium parts
facts: C919 first flight May 2017 with printed titanium parts | 28 cabin-door parts and 2 fan-inlet structural parts | FalconTech supplied 30 metal parts; BLT printed others
printer: Laser powder bed; FalconTech used foreign-brand machines
gains: Lighter titanium parts, shorter lead times, domestic capability
challenges: Early reliance on imported machines; mostly secondary structure
picture: C919 in flight / BLT printed part

title: BLT: a Chinese printer maker in Airbus series production
facts: Nov 2024, Zhuhai Airshow: new A320 metal O-ring work package for Airbus Atlantic | Printed in superalloy powder on BLT’s own S400 machine | Airbus A330 production approval for AM parts since 2018; A350 large-part agreement 2018
printer: Own BLT-S400 laser powder bed and own powders
gains: Vertical integration: 20 machine models, 1,000+ t powder a year
challenges: Quantities, value and part criticality not disclosed
sources: Metal AM, 20 Nov 2024; VoxelMatters; 3DPrint.com; Metal AM (Formnext 2025)
picture_source: metal-am.com › “BLT secures Airbus A320 serial production contract”

title: Airbus cabin: polymer parts at industrial scale
facts: 1,000+ printed parts on the first A350 delivered (Qatar Airways, Dec 2014) | Today 25,000+ flight parts a year for A320, A350 and A400M | Started in 2013 to de-risk the A350 delivery schedule
gains: −43% weight, −85% lead time, no minimum order quantity
challenges: Flame, smoke and toxicity compliance; strict material traceability

technology: Polymer · FFF and powder bed · Middle East
title: Etihad Engineering, Abu Dhabi: printing cabin parts in MRO
facts: 2017: first airline MRO to certify, print and fly 3D printed cabin parts (filament) | 2019: EASA approval for powder-bed polymer parts | Cabin defects fixed during line maintenance and C-checks
printer: EOS P 396 (PA 2241 FR, 340×340×600 mm); BigRep ONE
gains: Parts on site and on demand; jigs, fixtures and moulds
challenges: Design and production approval needed per technology
picture: Etihad 3D printing lab with EOS P 396

technology: Laser powder bed · nickel alloy IN718
title: Ariane 6: a one-piece printed injector head
facts: Injector head with 122 injection elements printed as one part instead of 248 | Developed for the Vinci upper-stage engine of Ariane 6 | The Vulcain 2.1 main engine also flies a printed gas generator
printer: EOS M 400-4 (four lasers), EOS NickelAlloy IN718
gains: −50% cost, build time ÷3, design iteration from ~6 months to days
challenges: Class-1 mission-critical part; internal cavities must stay clean in testing
sources: EOS / ArianeGroup case study; Develop3D; ArianeGroup; Cetim

title: Safran Additive Manufacturing Campus, Le Haillan (Bordeaux)
facts: €80 M, 12,500 m² centre of excellence opened October 2022 | R&D, engineering and series production of metal parts on one site | First 1,000 parts delivered to Safran Helicopter Engines within four months
printer: Laser powder bed incl. Renishaw RenAM 500Q; 8 printers at opening
gains: 4,000 parts in 2022, 8,000 in 2023, tens of thousands targeted in 2026
challenges: Much of the value lies in design and finishing, not only printing
sources: Safran, 7 Oct 2022; 3DPrint.com; Le Journal des Entreprises; TCT

title: US Navy FRCE: printing certified spares at the depot
facts: Fleet Readiness Center East, at Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, NC | First flight-certified metal parts printed in-house: three aluminium components | Installed on AH-1Z and V-22 (Marine Corps) and C-130
gains: Certified in under six months, a NAVAIR record
challenges: Each part still needs its own qualification; only three parts so far
sources: 3D Printing Industry / Pulse, 30 Apr 2026; TrendHunter, May 2026
